editorNote: This week's dispatch runs from the launch pad to the edge of the galaxy: Starship flew again and came home intact, while a Soyuz returned three crewmates after 241 days aloft. Farther out, the discoveries piled up — the first atmosphere on a rocky world in the habitable zone, a possible first moon beyond our solar system (and a giant one at that), and a clever scheme to find planets by their gravitational-wave whisper. NASA's Roman telescope, meanwhile, reached the pad months ahead of schedule.

stories.headline: SpaceX's Starship flies again — and lands the “softest splashdown” yet
stories.summary: On July 24 SpaceX launched the second flight of Starship V3 from Starbase, Texas, deploying 20 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites about 18 minutes in — its first look at them in flight. The Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf and the upper stage came to rest intact in the Indian Ocean, giving the first clear views of an undamaged heatshield. Two earlier attempts were scrubbed by a last-second engine abort and by weather.
stories.whyItMatters: Recovering an intact heatshield and deploying real payloads pushes Starship V3 from “can it fly” toward “can it work” — the reusability the whole program is built on.

stories.headline: For the first time, an atmosphere is found around a rocky planet in the habitable zone
stories.summary: Researchers report in Science (July 16) the first confirmed atmosphere around a rocky, Earth-like world in its star's habitable zone: LHS 1140 b, a super-Earth about 49 light-years away with roughly 1.7 times Earth's radius. Such an atmosphere could help regulate the planet's climate and let liquid water linger on its surface.
stories.whyItMatters: Rocky planets in habitable zones are no longer rare finds; confirming an atmosphere on one is the harder, more meaningful step toward asking whether a world could actually host life.

stories.headline: Astronomers may have spotted the first moon beyond our solar system — a Jupiter-sized one
stories.summary: Using the radial-velocity “wobble” method on the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope, astronomers report evidence of the first known exomoon — at least as massive as Jupiter — orbiting not a planet but a brown dwarf (CD-35 2772, about 33 Jupiter masses) some 71 light-years away. Other scientists caution the interpretation is still under debate.
stories.whyItMatters: If it holds up, it is the first satellite ever detected outside our solar system — and a giant one around a “failed star,” stretching what the word moon even means.

sourceLinks.title: First moon outside our solar system — or something weirder? (Space.com)

stories.headline: NASA's Roman telescope reaches the launch pad — about nine months early
stories.summary: NASA will hold a July 29 briefing to preview the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, now set to launch Aug. 30 from Kennedy Space Center on a SpaceX Falcon Heavy — roughly nine months ahead of schedule. Roman's field of view is at least 100 times Hubble's, built for sweeping cosmic surveys.
stories.whyItMatters: A Hubble-quality eye with a hundredfold wider view means surveys of dark energy, exoplanets and galactic structure at a scale Hubble could never cover.

stories.headline: After 241 days in orbit, a Soyuz brings three crewmates home to the steppe
stories.summary: Soyuz MS-28 undocked from the International Space Station and made a parachute landing on the Kazakh steppe, returning NASA astronaut Chris Williams and cosmonauts Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergei Mikaev after a 241-day mission — 3,856 orbits and more than 102 million miles since launching Nov. 27, 2025. It was the first spaceflight for Williams and Mikaev.
stories.whyItMatters: Long-duration stays like this are how space agencies bank the human-health data that future Moon and Mars trips will depend on.

sourceLinks.title: Chris Williams, crewmates return from station (NASA)

stories.headline: A new way to hunt planets: listen for them in gravitational waves
stories.summary: An Astrobites roundup describes how the planned LISA space observatory could detect giant planets circling double white dwarfs by the tiny shifts a planet imprints on the pair's gravitational-wave signal — a method akin to radial velocity but unaffected by stellar activity, and one that could in principle reach planets beyond the Milky Way.
stories.whyItMatters: Gravitational-wave detectors can “see” farther than telescopes, so this could eventually turn up the first planets outside our galaxy — places no current method can reach.
